summary: Children generate measurement data by measuring objects to the nearest half inch and to the nearest quarter inch on a ruler whose subdivisions they can read and name, then display the data on a line plot whose horizontal scale is partitioned into equal quarter-inch intervals (…2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3…). The demanding new skill is the SCALE: equal spacing, correct fraction ordering (2¼ < 2½ < 2¾), and recognising that 2½ sits at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4). A guiding practice is drawing the axis to true inch scale and keeping the ruler's quarter-inch ticks aligned with the plot's quarter marks so the subdivision of the tool and the subdivision of the axis are seen as the same partition of one unit. One X per object, and stack height means frequency, not length.
misconceptions: Spacing the fraction marks unequally or out of order — placing ½ midway but crowding or mis-ordering ¼ and ¾
Measuring 'to the nearest line' on the ruler without knowing the fraction that line represents, so a tick position is recorded rather than a measured value
Carrying over the value-vs-frequency habit — reading stack height as length
Treating ½ and 2/4 as different positions on the scale

activities.title: Measure to the nearest quarter and build the fractional scale
steps: Measure a set of ribbons or objects (about 5–6) against a ruler whose quarter-inch ticks are clearly marked and, at first, labelled with their fraction values (¼, ½, ¾).

For each object, name the quarter inch it rounds to out loud or in writing — e.g. 'this one is 2¾ inches', not 'the third line'; for one or two objects, also name the nearest half inch and notice that the two answers can be different.

Using the ruler to mark it, draw a number line at true scale (1 inch per whole number) that covers every measured length, and partition it into equal quarters between the whole numbers, so the marks run e.g. 2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3 in correct order and with equal spacing.
Place one X per object at its fractional value on the line.

Align the ruler directly under the true-scale plot, with the ruler's whole-inch marks under the matching whole numbers on the axis, so each ¼ tick on the ruler sits beneath the matching ¼ mark on the axis.
(Optional, on screen) Measure a ribbon that is 2¼ inches: drop its X and watch it settle one quarter-tick past 2, directly beneath the same tick on the ruler, making the shared subdivision visible.
Check ordering and equivalence explicitly: confirm 2¼ < 2½ < 2¾, and that 2½ lands at the same position as 2 2/4 (because ½ = 2/4).
Read the finished plot: e.g. 'how many objects were 2½ inches?' and 'how many were shorter than 2½?'
activities.insight: The subdivision on the ruler and the subdivision on the plot's axis are the same partition of one unit into equal quarters; a measured length maps to a position on an equal-interval scale, and ½ = 2/4 is one position, not two.

activities.title: Separate frequency from length
steps: On a completed fractional line plot, point to the axis position that gives an object's LENGTH and separately count the stacked Xs that give the FREQUENCY at that length.
Answer paired questions: 'How long is this object?' (read axis) versus 'How many objects were this long?' (count the stack).
Explain in your own words why a taller stack does not mean a longer object.
activities.insight: On a line plot the horizontal axis position is the measured value, while the height of a stack of Xs is how many objects share that value — these are two different quantities.

activities.title: Interpret and order a given fractional plot
steps: Given a finished fractional line plot, order the marked values 2¼, 2½, 2¾ from least to greatest.
Count how many objects fall at a given value (e.g. 'how many were 2½?').
Compare: how many objects were shorter than 2½, and how many were longer.
Confirm that 2½ and 2 2/4 name the same position on the scale (because ½ = 2/4).
activities.insight: A correctly built fractional scale can be read for order, counts, and comparisons, and equivalent fractions occupy the same position.

activities.title: Reference: name each quarter mark and show ½ = 2/4
steps: Study a labelled fractional line plot or fraction strip where each quarter mark is named (¼, ½, ¾).
Reveal or confirm that ½ equals 2/4 and that the half mark sits midway between adjacent whole numbers.
Use this as a reference while measuring and plotting, then set it aside once the scale can be built independently.
activities.insight: Each quarter tick has a nameable fraction value, and equivalent fractions (½ = 2/4) share one position; this naming supports accurate measuring and plotting.

checkQuestion: Give the child a ruler marked in quarter-inches and 6 objects. Say: 'Measure each to the nearest quarter inch and show them all on this line.' Provide an unmarked horizontal line. Watch how they subdivide the scale into quarters, whether the fraction marks are equally spaced and correctly ordered, and how they read the ruler to the nearest ¼.
checkAnswer: Subdivides the axis into equal quarter-inch intervals in correct order (…2, 2¼, 2½, 2¾, 3…), measures each object to the nearest quarter inch by reading the ruler's subdivisions, places one X per object at its fractional value, and can read the plot (e.g. 'how many were 2½ inches').
